comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Fillers 1 and 2 landed in 3d64f65. A contract run now fails on any warning or error the scenario did not declare it expects, and separately on any pane the window was told to show that never got a surface or never painted a frame. `check_bad_pane` declares `core.refused` and nothing else, so a second unrelated warning inside a scenario about a refusal still fails the run.

Both were replayed against the run logs of the two real bugs to check they bite:

- blank window (14:11): caught by the warning check (`pane.surface.deferred`, one record). Not caught by the paint check, because the pane did eventually paint once a split forced a republish. These read a whole run and cannot see how long something was broken for - worth knowing before trusting them.
- phantom pane (14:20): caught by both. 78 records the app itself called wrong, and `w1:p2` got a surface and never painted.

Filler 3 - invariants over sequences - is a habit rather than a change, and has two instances now: `cold_start.rs` and `resize.rs`. Left open for the part still undone: none of the daemon-backed tests starts from a state a user's daemon is actually in. They all build their world first, which is why a daemon holding nothing and a daemon holding a pane whose terminal died both had no coverage.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Filler 3 is now closed too, and one of the card's premises turned out to be wrong.

`crates/muster-seam/tests/inherited.rs` opens onto a session Muster did not build: a workspace somebody else created, two tabs, one zoomed, and a focused tab chosen by a person. It asserts invariants over whatever the window settles on - every pane on screen is typeable, every pane that exists is in the roster, none listed twice, and a pane in the tab nothing shows can still be reached. Verified to bite by making the roster report only what is on screen; it fails naming the pane it dropped.

Two things worth recording:

- **"A daemon holding a pane whose terminal died" is not a state.** herdr drops the pane from `pane.list` the moment its process goes, so a daemon holds a live pane or no pane. That case is the phantom pane (a_28TK7FIcF), which already has coverage.
- **A daemon holding nothing was already covered** by `cold_start.rs`.

Guarded against the failure this card is about: the arrangement is asserted before Muster sees it, because every check passes vacuously on a daemon holding one pane, and the hidden-pane half demands a hidden pane rather than skipping when there is none.

Raised on the way out: a_28XbMv3tn - the suite now starts enough concurrent daemons that a 10s deadline lost once during a full run and passed alone.

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
Three bugs in one session were all found by launching the app, and the contract tier ran the same scenarios and passed. The gap is not that we lack an end-to-end tier - it is what that tier asserts.

It asserts what the core decided, not what the window showed. `a clean machine gets a daemon and a workspace` checked `daemon.started`, `workspace.creating` and `typeable == true`, every one of which was true while the pane was blank. The window logged `pane.surface.deferred` with an accurate impact line and nothing read it.

Three fillers, cheapest first:

1. Fail a contract run on any warn or error record the scenario did not declare it expects. Our logs already carry the diagnosis - the DIS convention means a warn line names the impact - and nothing consumes them. This turns every log line we have already written into an assertion, including for bugs nobody has thought of.

2. Assert the shell's own outcome: for every pane a published view names, there is a `surface.create` and a `bridge.frame.first`. "The core said yes" and "a pane painted" are different claims and only the first is checked today.

3. Prefer invariants to sequences in the daemon-backed tests. `cold_start.rs` asserts that every pane a view names has a socket a bridge can dial, over whatever the view settled on - it caught the bug it was written for and two other paths that were wrong for the same reason. A test that replays one expected sequence would have caught one.

Also worth noting what none of the daemon-backed tests do: start from a daemon in a state a user's daemon is actually in. They all build their world first, so the states that bite - a daemon holding nothing, a daemon holding a pane whose terminal died - had no coverage at all.
title: 🧪 The suite is green while the window is broken
